summary: Herschel held posts with the Hanoverian Foot Guards (~1753–1758), County Durham Militia (1760–1761), Charles Avison (1761–1762), in Leeds (1762–1766), Octagon Chapel, Bath (1767–1780), Bath Philharmonia (1780–1782), and Observatory House (1782–1822).

A philosopher and religious studies scholar, James studied at Plymouth College and Harvard University (MD 1864–1869). He spent his academic career at Harvard, serving as physiology lecturer (1872), assistant professor (1876, 1880), and professor (1885).

An Indologist and linguist, Jones studied at Oxford and Middle Temple under teachers including I'tisam-ud-Din, Swinton, Ramachandra Vidyalankara, and Rāmalocana. He became a barrister, Chief Justice in Fort William (1783), and founded the Asiatic Society.

A scholar of Buddhist studies, Indology, and Tibetology, Ames studied at Caltech (MS) and the University of Washington (PhD) under Collett Cox and David Seyfort Ruegg. He held posts at Washington, CIIS, and JFK University (librarian, 2006).

A scholar of Buddhist studies, Japanology, and religious studies, Bodiford studied at Kansas, Tsukuba, Komazawa, and Yale (PhD under Stanley Weinstein). He taught at Davidson and Iowa before serving as professor at UCLA (~1992–2021; emeritus ~2021).

Gorvine, a scholar of Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies, earned his BA at Connecticut College and his MA and PhD (2006) at the University of Virginia, where he was supervised by David Germano.

Smart studied at the University of Glasgow (~1906–1911) and the University of Cambridge / Trinity College (~1911–1914). He later held academic appointments at Cambridge (~1919–1937) and Glasgow (~1937–1959).

Active in history and archaeology, Muir was educated at Kilmarnock Academy, the University of Edinburgh (~1834–1836), and Haileybury (~1836–1837). He later served as Vice-Chancellor of the University of Edinburgh (~1885–1903).
A scholar in Buddhist studies, Chu completed an MA in 2006 at the University of California, Los Angeles, where he was supervised by Robert E. Buswell Jr.

Specializing in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology, Price was Professor of Hindūstaní at Fort William College (~1813–1830) and a member of the Asiatic Society and the Royal Asiatic Society.

A religious studies and history scholar, Hutchison earned degrees from Oxford and Yale (PhD 1956). He held posts at Yale, Hunter College, American University, Wisconsin-Madison, and taught at Harvard University beginning in 1968.

A Japanologist and Buddhist studies scholar, LaFleur studied at Calvin University, Michigan, and Chicago (PhD 1973). He held posts at Princeton, UCLA, UC Berkeley, and served as professor at the University of Pennsylvania (~1990–2010).

A linguist and religious studies scholar, Harper studied at Muskingum and Yale under William Dwight Whitney. He taught at Denison and Yale before serving as president of the University of Chicago (1891–1906) and Bradley University (~1897–1906).

A historian and Indologist, Robertson studied divinity at the University of Edinburgh (1733–1741). He was appointed Principal of Edinburgh in 1762 and held memberships in the Royal Society of Edinburgh and the Russian Academy of Sciences.

Roxburgh earned MD degrees at Edinburgh and Aberdeen/Marischal College. He served as superintendent at Samalkot Experimental Garden (1781) and Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden (1793), and was Keeper at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh.
A scholar of Indology, Buddhist studies, and linguistics, Stede taught extensively while holding academic posts at SOAS and the University of London from ~1928 to 1949.

Active in religious studies, Buddhist studies, and psychology, Van Gordon founded the Awake to Wisdom Centre for Meditation and Mindfulness Research and was a research psychologist at Nottingham Trent University (attested 2015).
Working in Indology and religious studies, Ward studied at Ewood Hall Academy (1797). He served as a missionary at the Serampore Mission (~1800–1823) and founded Serampore College in 1818.

An Indologist and historian, Hunter studied at Glasgow, Paris, and Bonn. He served in the Indian Civil Service (~1862–1887), became Vice-Chancellor of the University of Calcutta (1886), and vice-president of the Royal Asiatic Society (~1895–1900).

A scholar of Tibetology, Sinology, and Buddhist studies, Rockhill studied at Lycée Condorcet and École Spéciale Militaire de Saint-Cyr (~1871–1873). He was taught by Léon Feer and Philippe-Édouard Foucaux.
